text: This chapter is about database design — and every design starts the same way: you have to actually create the table. CREATE TABLE is the single most fundamental statement in all of T-SQL, and it's where this chapter begins.

Create table dbo dot LessonDemo, open paren, DemoID int not null, label nvarchar 50 not null, notes nvarchar 200 null, close paren. A schema-qualified name, then a comma-separated list of column definitions. Each column gets a name, a data type, and a nullability rule.

DemoID int not null means every row must have a value there — SQL Server rejects any insert or update that tries to leave it empty. Notes nvarchar 200 null means that column is allowed to stay empty. Decide this at design time; it's much harder to fix once real data is sitting in the table.

You can also define a primary key right inline, directly after a column's type: DemoID int not null primary key. That's a preview of the very next chapter topic — for now, just recognize the shape. Primary keys guarantee uniqueness and not null together, for whichever column you mark this way.

Insert into dbo dot LessonDemo4, values 1, First row, 1. Select star from dbo dot LessonDemo4. Drop table dbo dot LessonDemo4. Notice every demo in this chapter runs against a table you created yourself — never against a real AdventureWorks2012 table. Practice structural changes on scratch tables only.
Next lesson: ALTER TABLE, for adding and modifying columns on a table that already exists.
